lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. It seems that in today's political climate, we are discouraged from thinking critically and rather conditioned to see our side as the right side and the other side as the enemy. But the truth is, no political party or politician has a monopoly on truth, wisdom, or morality. Every party or politician, no matter how well-intentioned, has weaknesses If we can't admit when our party or leaders get it wrong, or when ones we don't support get it right, then we aren't truly thinking critically. We're just cheering for a team. That doesn't mean we have to abandon our political beliefs. It means we shouldn't support a party platform or politic— it doesn't mean we shouldn't support a party platform or politician. In fact, we should. But it does mean we should be willing to ask hard questions challenge assumptions, and hold our leaders accountable, even when they're the ones we voted for. Thinking critically about politics means going beyond headlines, partisan talking points, and emotional reactions to engage with issues thoughtfully and objectively. Our allegiance should not come at the cost of supporting or defending every decision that is made. This removes accountability and ends up hurting all of us in the long run. No politician or party is perfect. It's important we hold all leaders accountable, not just the ones on the other side. By thinking critically about politics, we strengthen democracy and ensure that our choices are guided by reason, not just rhetoric. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk
lines.title: Senior Manager, Finance
lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor, members of council. I am pleased to be presenting the city's 2025 financial plan to highlight some of the main items that are planned for the upcoming year. The annual budget cycle is almost a continuous process. For the 2025 budget year, it started early in 2024. Throughout the process, input is provided by staff, management, and council. The financial plan being presented today is based on the recommendations of council provided at their final review in November. Some of the highlights for 2025 include a municipal mill rate of 14.4 mills, which remains the same as 2024. 2025 was, however, a reassessment year, so overall municipal taxes will increase by the same percentage as the assessment increase for each property. Utility rates will increase by an average of 3%. Thank you. While residential garbage collection rates will increase by 4.5%. Fees for permits are up 5%, and land use application fees will increase by 2.5%. The overall capital program for 2025 is budgeted at $36.6 million. Some of the larger budgeted projects include the completion of the event center The Loewen PTH 12 intersection renewal, Park Road West force main twinning, as well as the Millwork Drive sewer replacement. Overall projected revenues for 2025 are just over $42 million. Similar to other years, property taxes are the city's largest source of revenue, accounting for just over half of the overall revenue amount. For 2025, there was a property value growth of 14.9%. Commercial properties make up about 24% of the total property values in the city, and with the provincial portioning system, a lower portion of residential property values are subject to property tax than commercial property values. Thank you. As I mentioned earlier, the property tax rate of 14.4 mills is unchanged from 2024. 54% of budgeted municipal revenues are from property taxes. $22.7 million is to be raised by property taxes in 2025, and $21.6 million of this is via mill rate. The city is also required to collect the education and school taxes on behalf of the province and Hanover School Division. As in previous years, this is projected to make up roughly half of the total tax revenue collected. The average market value for a dwelling in Steinbach is roughly $250,000. Based on this and the budgeted municipal mill rate, the average city property tax bill works out to roughly $135 a month. In addition to regular property taxes, supplementary property taxes are levied on new construction or where there was an addition or improvement to increase the value of the property. This is expected to provide an additional $675,000 in 2025. Federal and provincial operating grants have also been a consistent source of revenue for the city. The provincial per capita tax sharing grant is expected to provide $4.6 million in 2025, while the federal gas tax grant will provide just over $1 million. One of the main non-tax revenues for the city is from user fees. These are fees paid by those who benefit from the service provided. Some services compete with the open market, but a number of the rates are subsidized for programs to be accessible. Development in Steinbach stayed strong in 2024 with just under $105 million in total permit values. This activity is expected to continue into 2025 and beyond. Now we will look at some of the programs that are funded by these revenues. Overall, the expenses are equal to the projected revenues at just over $42 million. Some 2025 programs include waste reduction and recycling at just over $1.1 million, support for the Jake Epp Public Library at $455,000, the beautification program at $286,000, and various other programs as listed. Every year, the city provides grants for various organizations throughout the city. In 2025, these grants total just over $1 million, with the recipients as listed. One of the largest city expenses is that of our employees. The total labor cost, including benefits, for 2025 is budgeted at $12 million, or roughly a third of the city's operating budget. Of this total, the aquatic centre makes up about 19% of the total labour hours, the largest of any city department. Protective services includes RCMP, 47 firefighters and 8 fire trucks, As well as a community services officer to enforce city bylaws. The total cost of these services is budgeted at $5.6 million for the upcoming year. The city currently has almost 145 kilometres of road surface. The maintenance for this infrastructure can depend significantly on the weather in any given year, And for 2025 is expected to cost $3.2 million. Solid waste services. We provide both curbside and on-demand pickup services to both residential and commercial properties. The cost of providing these services is expected to reach $3.3 million for the upcoming year, which is funded by user fees. Thank you. Our primary recreation facilities include the aquatic centre, arena, A.D. Penner Park, curling rink, and soccer park, as well as various green space and parks around the city. The expected cost of operating and maintaining these facilities is budgeted at $5.8 million for 2025. Thank you. Both the number of customers serviced by the water and wastewater utility and the length of the underground infrastructure network continue to grow. The expected cost to maintain this infrastructure and provide the utility services is expected to be $4.7 million in 2025. Thank you. In addition to the typical operating expenses that the city regularly incurs, larger projects also require significant funding. Some of this comes from reserve funds that have been saved in previous years, while other projects will require debt funding. Some of the main projects for the upcoming year include equipment replacement, the Park Road West force main twinning, The completion of the events centre and the PTH 12 Loewen intersection. Total capital program for the year is expected to be just over $36.5 million. The city will periodically issue debt in order to add or renew various infrastructure or facilities throughout the city. Each loan will fund a specific project. In 2025, 4 projects have a debt component: the event centre construction, the Loewen Boulevard PTH 12 intersection, fire department ladder truck, and the force main twinning. This is expected to create $13.25 million of new debt while $2.6 million of previously issued debt will be paid off. The city continues to use a 5-year amortization term for all of its debt. allowing us to borrow at lower interest rates than if a longer term was used. Our average interest rate for 2025 is just over 4%, while the debt balance at the end of the year is expected to be $21.5 million. Payments that are required for previously issued debt will total $3.1 million in 2025. Of this amount, $443,000 is interest. Funding for these debt payments is raised through property taxation, and for 2025, $1.945 mils will be required to raise the necessary funds. This equates to 13.5% of the total city tax rate. And finally, a longer-term overview of some of the expected requirements in future years. The 2025 program is currently budgeted at $36.6 million, which includes infrastructure renewal, the completion of the event center, and the force main twinning. Beyond that, programs of $18.2 million, $58.2 million, and $56.5 million are currently estimated for the following 3 years. That concludes the presentation of the 2025 financial plan. Thank you, members of council. If there are any questions, I can answer them now.

lines.text: Hello, I'm [Resident 1], 534 Wilson Street. Okay, I have a question relating to the 2025 budget. What I can see is our past audited statements, and for the period from 2010 to 2022, the city balance sheet shows the book value of our city's infrastructure has been declining compared to what it originally cost to build. To me, that would indicate that we've not been keeping up. Now, the new event centre, a major capital project, makes it kind of hard to determine what's happening in '23 and '24. But did this trend continue or did it not? So my question is, what are the means and measures that the city uses to ensure that we're not falling behind and that our infrastructure remains strong and functional for the long term? Thank you. Without burdening future generations with avoidable costs?

While the provincial requirement is that it include a 5-year look ahead, the City of Steinbach has tried to maintain anywhere between a 7 and a 10-year look ahead as far as an official document. It's appeared in various formats over the past decades. And the city employs an engineering department of 4 staff, along with the expertise within the city's engineering department, is the ability to analyze models, for example, to, to determine is the city's infrastructure capacity able to maintain existing services to existing built-up areas and also be able to grow and expand to accommodate new service areas that do come up from time to time. And through various mathematical models, that's the best way that the city can use that data that we have, as well as industry averages, to determine, you know, planning for the future, as well as how does the city address the existing infrastructure that's already installed. Thank you. And be able to maintain it. Fortunately, the city of Steinbach, from an organization and from public infrastructure, is a fairly young community. I believe the first sewer and water lines were installed in the late 1950s. Relative to urban centers, many of them across Canada, they have infrastructure systems that are well over 100 years old. Thank you. And certainly the challenges in maintaining those kinds of infrastructure systems are significantly more complex and challenging with that kind of aging. And with that more recent type of infrastructure, the city has been able to take advantage of newer and more resilient materials such as PVC, which tend to have a fairly predictable and longer service life than some of the older materials that used to be used. Other than that, the city has also begun using different models to evaluate its pavement infrastructure, where we have consultants come in to do a review and actually analyze the relative repair index of all the city streets. Go ahead. If I recall correctly, out of a total available points rating of 100, the most recent review of the city's concrete and asphalt streets indicated a rating of 72, which is considered very good, and relative to other communities or other urban centres is above average. I will acknowledge that as the city grows and as its infrastructure ages, there is always a greater and greater challenge to be able to allocate the appropriate financial and professional resources to maintain its infrastructure. Even though the book value of the assets, as you mentioned, appear to be declining on a net basis, again, relative to other comparable cities that the city is aware of, the city's Representative information, and as far as the overall life remaining of the assets that it has installed, again, is above average as compared to other urban jurisdictions. And I remember when we got the previous ladder truck, that was a long time ago, and these upgrades have to happen. The Forest Main 20 borrowing's at $2.75 million. Of course, we need to make sure that, that we have the necessary water capacity for a growing city. And $5 million of this year's debt is also for the event center. The event center, of course, is the largest project that we've ever done in our history. Total cost when you put it all together is about $74 million, and the city is contributing just over $30 million of that in total. Obviously significant contributions from the private sector and other levels of government, but the city is contributing the largest portion of that $74 million. And so what this does tell us is that the old maxim that growth pays for itself is not true, because obviously if the city was not growing, we wouldn't be having to do a lot of these things. If the city was not growing, we would not be building an event centre. If it was not growing, we wouldn't need to upgrade Highway 12 because the traffic would just stay at the same level. If the city wasn't growing, we wouldn't have to upgrade our water supply capacity in order to deal with— to make sure we have the necessary sewer and water capacity. These are all challenges that come with a growing city. If the city wasn't growing, we wouldn't have to, on a periodic basis, increase the number of RCMP officers. Madam Mayor, And of course, one of the challenges this year is that we're not increasing the total number of officers. But as you've probably read about in the news, because this has gotten a fair bit of coverage, RCMP costs are not controlled by the city. All that we're able to do is we're able to say the number of officers that we wish to have, but the actual amount that, that it costs for them, that's determined in a bargaining process between the federal government and the RCMP union. That's not something the city has direct control over. Control over, and that obviously has been a, has been a point of frustration. There is extra money that's being spent on public works because we have to make sure that we keep up with upgrades within the city. And Parks and Rec, a large part of that increase is because we do have to contribute towards the operating costs of the, of our event center. We have the reality that we've, we have fewer reserves now than we did a couple of years ago, and that's because we made tough choices when the event Centre cost went up, which we knew that was a possibility. But obviously during the pandemic, costs went up a lot in a lot of things in terms of dealing with any kind of construction. And so we had to use those reserves. And that means that when planning a budget, we're not able to access reserves as much because much of that has already been used for the event centre, which means that for necessary infrastructure items, we have to take it out of the— we have to take it out of our— Revenue. It comes out of the operating budget or debt, and of course that impacts taxes. The mill rate that we're taking is being left at the same at $14.4 million, which does mean that there is an overall increase. The property value growth is 14.9%. That's not all tax increase. The growth does pay for some of that. Around 4% or so is typically what we have year over year. Okay. But then obviously the balance, you know, that, that does work out to be a tax increase. And so the debt payments just alone is $1.35 million more than it was last year. And obviously there is no way to paper over that. We can't hide that. That is just the reality. The reason I asked the questions that I did of our financial individual, Brian— Mr. Hrehirchuk, the reason I asked those questions about, well, what if we were to do the boring over a longer period of time, Is that is always an option. We could change the borrowing policy and we could borrow over 10, 15, or 20 years. But here is the harsh reality. If we do that, we can save money in the short term right now on this particular budget, but we will— taxpayers will still pay more for those same projects in the overall term because the interest rate that's being paid is higher. And when you're paying it all off over a longer period of time, Thank you. It's, uh, you just— you are— it does cost more. And plus, you've got the reality that we're burdening future councils with the cost of projects that, uh, that we're taking on now. And so instead of paying something off in 5 years, you're paying it off in 15 or 20 years, which means that you've got less fiscal room to take care of necessary infrastructure projects. And so I don't think that changing that policy would make sense at this point. Yes, right now When we're taking on $13.25 million in new debt and only retiring $2.6 million, that means that we're taking on over $10 million of new debt this year, which means significant debt payments, which is impacting the tax rate. And that is a challenge. But most of the time, in most years, that 5-year borrowing policy, we see the benefits of it. And so— and we are in a much better fiscal situation now, having that policy for the last 30 years plus. Thank you. than if we did not have that policy in place. And so I think it would be short-sighted if we tried to say that, well, we'll try to hide the increase here, we'll just put it, you know, we'll borrow everything over a longer period of time, because that's not fair to our, to our residents, because then that will just end up costing more in the long run. I look at the pro— the programs that we're— that we are spending money on. These are important programs. We are prioritizing infrastructure. Which is the number one priority of any municipality, or at least it should be. No municipality should be cutting infrastructure in order to pay for recreation projects or, you know, other sort of grant programs and such. We are not doing that. I'm very proud of our infrastructure spending and the work that we're doing in terms of the underground infrastructure, fixing our roads. We're going to keep doing that, and we're not going to stop doing that because we're faced with some tough choices. Based on, you know, other projects that we're doing, the events centre being an obvious one, we are not going to put those projects on hold and the necessary maintenance and upgrades because of the fact that we have some significant costs from our new events centre. And so it is a challenging budget, but I believe it is the right path forward. And I don't paper it over. It is difficult, but I think it is the right path to go. So I move— I would support Thank you, Councillor Switzer.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I'm not going to reiterate. Councillor Switzer did a good job of summarizing it. But I do want to say that none of us take this lightly. I know myself, I have spent considerable time thinking how, like, what can we do to, you know, lower the mill rate? What can we do so the tax increase is less? But there is not frivolous spending. Thank you. I think it's important to note that in terms of the capital spending in this budget, we're doing it the same way we always do. We run a tight ship, and I know this council, for as long as I've been on council, has just really worked hard to toe the line. And in spite of the tax increase, we are still doing that with this. It is really an adjustment that needs to be made. It's a new normal in terms of the increase. When I think of construction costs And what we were quoted on a lot of projects 5 years ago to when we're at— they actually come to fruition, costs have doubled, tripled, and it's just not feasible that we could continue doing what we're doing with the costs having increased as they have without this tax increase. Again, I just want to reiterate that we genuinely believe this is necessary and we do not take this lightly. Thank you. And it's just something we need to do. And hopefully— the other thing I would just like to point out, I've often thought, you know, maybe when, you know, this is going to be painful for 5 years because we have the rec centre debt payment, but, you know, that's not even half of what the debt payment is going to be. So I can't really blame it on that. And further, even when that debt expires, we've got major projects in terms of like a water treatment facility that's coming down the pipe that's probably going to be no joke, $100 million. This is just kind of the new normal we're operating with in terms of costs and things we need to do for our city.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much. Anything further, council? Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I just want to first start off with, and this is something that I get asked a lot, and it's this— we're talking about our budget and they say, well, the mill rate didn't go up, so the taxes won't go up. The mill rate is essentially a multiplier on your assessed value of your house. So if the value of your house goes up, even though we hold the mill rate even, it's the multiple— the multiplier is still the same, but the assessed is up. So I just wanted to get that out, out in the public so to understand when, when we say that there's, there's no mill rate increase, that doesn't necessarily mean that your taxes are staying the same. Inversely also, we've, we've worked very hard over the last numerous years to hold the line on no net increases. So We've decreased the mill rate. We've tried to keep that tax burden on the on the individual at at a net even, and the reality is municipal governments are in the service industry. Being in service, you have to ask well what are we going to cut then? And service industry is one of the hardest hit by inflation. Inflation in terms of wages, inflation in terms of product. And so with the service— with us being in service industry and being hit for numerous years, we were able to hold the line. But eventually you see the reserves go to a point where we say this is, this is getting uncomfortable. We need to start— we need to make sure that the future is being built up. And unfortunately, that is where we are. We are at that point today. But to highlight this, within our service industries, we have $22.6 million budgeted out of a $42 million budget. It's a significant amount that's going to services. So you have to ask, do we cut police and fire? Do we cut transportation? Do we cut solid waste? Recreation services? Water? None of these, in my opinion, are on the table to reduce the budgets to because we need to ensure that the quality of life for our individuals is continually getting better as the city grows, not decreasing. With regards to possible solutions of spreading the debt out further, Mr. Hrehirchuk highlighted it that there's $3.1 million in debt payments this year, but $443,000 in interest. That's a significant amount of interest, and that's only on a 5-year amortization. So we need to make sure that we're keeping that— our debts as minimal as possible on as short a term as possible. And so that does then mean when we've come into the stressors of what's gone on in terms of inflation over the last couple years, eventually the egg is going to crack and we're going to have to open it up. Having said that though, part of being able to avoid debt is we are putting 5 Allotting $5 million towards reserves to continue to build those back up to make sure that there is safety and there is a little bit more, more room within the budget to account for these things in the future as well, so that hopefully significant tax increases would never have— won't have to happen, or at least not in the near future, without something being linked directly to large infrastructure. So it is— Thank you. unfortunate. I don't— I'm not happy with it, but I'm also not pleased with the way that a lot of prices have happened over the last, last 2, 3 years. And this is, this is the first time that the resident is seeing it on their property tax bill.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: So, thank you very much. Anything further, Council?

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. As Councillor Zwaagstra has said, this is a challenging budget. So thank you very much for all the work that you've done on that. You know, you've presented the revenue, you presented the expenses, and we can see that our administration is really good at stewards of the taxpayers' money. Thank you. So my hat goes off to our administration and finances. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much. Anything in closing?

lines.text: Nope.

lines.text: Well, council, great comments. Lots have been said and lots of great things have been said. I too, I have a challenge with this budget. Honestly, I don't like tax increases. I don't like them. And we've done very, we've done a great job Most years when there have been assessment and value assessment and increase in assessment, we've brought the mill rate down to net zero. Looking forward to this year, it looks like that's not a possibility with the— all these things that we look at, as Councillor Switzer said, are important. RCMP is important. Public safety is important. Fire trucks, ladder trucks are important. Public works, maintaining our equipment in public works and doing, getting projects done, smaller projects done without debentures is very important too. And I think that's where a lot of these costs are coming from. And of course, the extra, debt that is being occurred through projects that we have done. We've been very aggressive with projects that have to be done as we're growing. We have lots of cars on roads. We've got— we have to upgrade the roads. We have to make sure that they can carry those people to where they need to go. So yes, as much as we— as much as this is difficult, as much as we spend time, I think, The person that's going to be happiest about this meeting is Mr. Horarchuk because he's going to have to— he can stop meeting with me now about this budget. They're tight. So there's just, there's just no way of looking at it. Councillor Susan Penner brought something up about the Chamber of Commerce grant, and I think that needs to be relooked at at the next study session. That's a grant that's significant. It keeps growing. That's tied to assessment and growth in business, and that's always growing every year. So I think that's something we need to look at as well. Thank you for bringing that up. Thank you. But council, I will, I will support this, this motion, and I'll call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Thank you. Okay, council, we'll move on to item B. This is variance 2025-02. This is referring to 268 and 274 Home Street. This is on page 29 of our package. Mr. Warkentin, could you please introduce this file?

lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: With respect to the application, this particular proposal was the subject of a rezoning in, in early 2024, and the proposal was to seek council approval to rezone the property from RLD, residential low density, to RMD, residential medium density. That public hearing was held on March 19th, 2024, and ultimately due to the number of Thank you. There were no objections registered at that public hearing. A further public hearing held by the Manitoba Municipal Board was held in August of this year, and evidence presented at the board hearing confirmed that the site would have an underground parking level plus 3 stories for residential units. And pursuant to the application, there is some uncertainty at the time of writing of this report I would like to move that the application be deferred as there was no available information to determine what potentially was, in fact, the intention of the developer and to what degree the proposed 4th story consisting of the parking level of the proposed development was intended to look like. It is recommended that city council request from the proponent to confirm how much of the underground parking is in fact planned to be below grade and how much is planned to be above grade. And subsequent to that, if approval is contemplated by council and council is satisfied with the evidence provided, it is also recommended that any approval be subject to any conditions council feels are appropriate. subject to a development agreement and to any new information that may be provided at this public hearing.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warkentin. Okay, at this time, I will close the council meeting, open the public hearing. Is the applicant here today? Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)
lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Mayor and council. Thank you for having me. My name is Luke Wiebe. I live at 3001736E Hirschfeld Road. I represent Kingdom Home Building, and this may be one of the quicker presentations I've ever done.

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)
lines.text: I have an outline on page 2, a variance request with height difference and conclusion. As Mr. Warkentin alluded, when I sent in my information originally with the hearing, public hearing that we did roughly 1 year ago, I had this, this 3D rendering here, which I still I have in my presentation today.

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)
lines.text: You can see that the parkade, it's underground, but it's not fully underground. That was, that was how I presented it. I asked the, the engineer design consultant what the depth would be because this is for illustration purposes, and he estimated roughly 6.5 feet, 6 feet underground, and then the rest would be above. It's roughly a meter above grade till the main floor height of the First floor of the apartment buildings. So if this was a 3-storey building in the National and Manitoba Building Code, it would still be considered under the building code as a 3-storey building with an underground parkade. However, in your City of Steinbach bylaws, a 3-storey building with parking underground is still considered a 4-storey, whether it's underground or above grade. So that's why I need to apply for a variance for that. Okay. So the building design and style and overall component of the site is not changing. So the purpose of the variance is, as I said, to allow a heated parkade to be constructed under 3 storeys of residential units. So I asked the design consultant to tell me what the height difference would be. He said it's approximately 53 foot 9. This is assuming I didn't do a flat roof, which is still possible. However, if I do a roof similar to this, it would be 53 foot 9 to the highest peak from the side of the building if done with main floor parking, which is on your left, and approximately 47 feet if done partially underground as originally illustrated at the original hearing there, rezoning hearing. So it's a difference of 6 foot 9. I am personally not partial to either. They're both good options. They have pros and cons if you, if you want to know. Okay. Or ask, feel free to. Administration has indicated that the variance to allow a 4th story RMD for parking, which the city has done on several occasions in RMD for a parking garage, is required whether it's a 3-story with parking partially underground or 4-story with main floor parkade. So my request today is that council approve the variance to permit the 4th story for parking and the decision whether partially underground or main level be decided through the development agreement and engineered construction plan submission process. This will allow the engineers, both my own and the city engineers, as well as the design team, the time they require to confirm which options make the most sense for this projected building design. I would like to say that I'm not changing the overall— the design of this project at all. However, we're not required to submit completed construction plans until we get to the development stage, development agreement stage, and construction plan review with your— Your council. engineer department, planner, and building inspectors. So that is why that is something that I can't confirm, because I'm not the, the professional that draws those plans. Any questions?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Um, are there any questions for the applicant? Go ahead.

lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: So just to confirm, you're not increasing units? I think there's a perception maybe that by adding a 4th story, you're adding another level of units. Nope. The number of units stays the same? What you're just requesting is the 6-foot—

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)
lines.text: The number of units, yes. So the number of units, the number of units will— has never been 100% assured yet because it's always dependent on the parking. So whatever our parking with the final construction plan, when I speak with Lacey in the end, when I submit those plans, I'll already know. But that, that's what, that's what will dictate the amount of units. So they will not be different because I'm not adding a level.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: It's not an extra—

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)

But like I said, there's both have the pros and cons as far as from a cost and time construction and all that. But yeah.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. I do have a question for administration. Is that something like deciding whether the parking is grade level or underground, is that something that will come out in the development agreement or is that something that the developer should have decided here tonight?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: The opinion of administration is that that is a very specific design question that should only be be decided by and communicated by the developer to council so that council can make a decision whether or not to approve the requested 4th story based on all of the information. That would be a component that would be unusual to be in a development agreement, in my opinion.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Okay, then in that, in that contents, We will ask you to give us direction whether it will be grade parking or underground parking.

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: We're looking at, so that we can make a decision based on the information we have, we need to know, are you going to do grade parking or underground parking? That is the way I understand it from our administration.

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.)

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, so you're, you're going to be— I'm fine with that. You're inclined to go with the original, which was underground?

lines.speaker: Luke Wiebe
lines.title: Applicant (developer)
lines.label: Luke Wiebe (Applicant (developer), Kingdom Home Building Inc.) [medium]
lines.text: Yep.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. So normally in our packages, there's a recommendation from administration as to whether we should approve or not. Your recommendation indicated that there's some uncertainty here because we don't have the specifics as far as what was being presented. With what the applicant has presented, saying that he is going if this was approved, it would be the underground parking. Based on that information, what is the official recommendation from administration on this variance?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: That was one component. There was some uncertainty based on the information that administration reviewed from the applicant. Now that the applicant has explicitly stated that the requested variance approval for the 4th story of the subject property Administration is satisfied that that is clear. Therefore, if council is comfortable with that 4th requested store being underground parking, if council chooses to approve, that would be a recommendation of administration.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor

lines.title: Mayor

lines.text: Open for discussion. It actually changes a lot I think the challenge is— I think the challenge is— For me, and I don't want to go too much because we're in, in this, but, uh, then we're not discussing the, the principles of a 4th story being underground versus actually adding a 4th story. So one is this is a principle of something that we're moving towards in our bylaws already, of a 4th story that's underground is— should just be allowed, versus this is now changing the entire dynamic of— it's essentially almost another public hearing, uh, which I voted against last time.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: So spell out your friendly amendment to me.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion— that the motion is to approve subject to the parking garage be no more than a meter above grade.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Sure.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Fine.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I'm in favor of this motion with the amendment. Due to the fact that this is something that we are working towards, that this doesn't change what was already voted for and approved for by council in terms of the project that is— was presented at that time. It was already approved. Having said that, I do want to greatly send my thanks and appreciation to the community that's come out not only once, but twice in some cases to the municipal board hearing as well. Thank you. It's exhausting being in these meetings sometimes, especially in the gallery and waiting for your turn. So I want to extend my appreciation to that. But this isn't about the project now at this point for my vote to approve. This is about the principle of 4th story underground shouldn't be considered a story.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council?

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I will take a different approach here. I've heard both sides. I think it's important to listen carefully to the applicant and administration and, of course, to the neighbourhood, I'll be voting against the variance. There's a couple of reasons. Obviously, as Councillor Penner had alluded, there was an initial vote on the rezoning itself, and we're not relitigating that right now, but that was a close vote. That was 4-3. I had voted against it because I have concerns— I had concerns at the time about this being rezoned to medium density because I didn't think it would fit into the neighbourhood. Nevertheless— Alderman Carra. The rezoning has been approved. So that is not what is up for debate right now. I cannot relitigate that. However, we do have a variance request, which in most cases I would tend to agree with Councillor Penner that— both Councillor Penners, frankly, on this point— that having an underground or partially underground or 3/4 underground or whatever number we're coming up with here, I'm not really sure, but whatever, having the story be I understand that. Parking as opposed to the residences, when that's at least partially underground, I understand that that's actually a fairly reasonable thing to allow, and then you still have 3 regular stories of residential. Here's my issue. I had concerns with this being rezoned medium density in the first place because I had serious questions as to that level of density increase in that area. By allowing this variance, we're allowing more density, more residential than would otherwise happen. Because if this were denied, yes, the project would need to be redesigned, and inevitably that would mean fewer units. That would mean less impact in the neighbourhood. Potentially even maybe not as many stories. Who knows? Because it would require redesign. In terms of it really would have been better if this variance had been dealt with at the time of the initial application, the rezoning. That's normally— that tends to be what happens here where we have a debate and a vote on the rezoning and on the variance request because normally a project is presented in a more full and complete sense. I appreciate the fact that the applicant has now given us some— a more complete version here in terms of what he is proposing to do. But again, just the very fact that we're sort of going back and forth about, you know, how far underground is it going to be and this sort of thing indicates to me that this thing is not settled. And so if not allowing the variance means that there are fewer residences, less impact to the neighbourhood, and that would mean fewer cars, considering that I had concerns with the rezoning to begin with, I'm not interested in the variance that adds to the problem by having more dwelling units than would otherwise be allowed. Hence, I'll vote against the variance.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. If council recalls, when the rezoning came up last time, I was against it.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: We heard a number of neighbourhood— it wasn't a usual council meeting where just 2 or 3 neighbours came and objected. We had a large number of people in the area objecting to this building in the area, and I voted against it at that time. And as Councillor Zwaagstra has said, You know, for a number of points that were raised, I agree with what he said. I, again, I can't go along with the motion in this case.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Any closing?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Yeah, this is interesting to me. I've been on council for, I think it's 12 or 14 years, something like that now, and in my entire time when we're looking at our official community plan and planning for the downtown, we try and want to increase density in the downtown. We want to keep our downtown vibrant. We want infill multifamily. Everything we've kind of talked about, this project represents. And now when we have a project that represents what we're going for and actually falls in line with those plans, you know, half of council isn't supporting it. And I find that interesting. This project does represent— it is basically a buffer between Thank you. It's single-family and, you know, more commercial with the hospital and event centre there. It allows for walkability, which is something we want. We want more density downtown. It will decrease car usage because people are in walkable distance downtown. So I just think this is— I understand anytime a project like this comes to us in an area where there's single family, it's difficult for the neighborhood. But at the same time, when we're talking about redeveloping the downtown, a project like this is exactly what we're looking for. So I, I'm pleased to support it, and I think it's going to be a good addition and something we, we value in our area downtown there.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Well, Council, this has been a A bit of a confusing file, one with the developer didn't come with a clear desire of what he wanted to do, but that was dealt with at the meeting. I think that worked out okay. You know, council, we all know that when, up until 3 years ago, we lived in the downtown and we were surrounded by multifamily. Yes. They were all 4 stories. Underground parking, 3 stories up. Yes, it does affect your shade, and— but we adjusted and we bought a bunch of hostas, and they love shade, and we had a beautiful backyard regardless. I think there can be beauty amongst multifamily as well. It worked very well. Thank you. Yeah. Strategic planting of trees, and during summer, we didn't even know there was multifamily behind us 'cause the trees filled it in so nicely. And it does work. You can live harmoniously with multifamily like we're looking for to densify our downtown, and single-family dwellings can live side by side, and it can work very, very nicely. And I know that we, 'cause we did it, we did it for 11 years downtown here. Yeah. It worked very well. The painful part was when the building came in, the thought of the building, that was the worst part. Once it was there, the whole neighborhood would adjust around the building. It worked out very, very nice. We had 3 36-plex around us. And so that was, that's considerably higher than this density. And as far as did we notice traffic, not really. Downtown's always busy. There's always lots of traffic downtown. We didn't notice necessarily extra traffic just because the downtown was like, was being built up. So I will support this. To the motion as was amended. 'Cause I do think this is the long term for this region, this area. I do believe it'll be a lot of institutional, and I think it'll be— there'll be more multifamily in the long term. I mean, you look— I'm looking 15, 20 years down the road. I'm not looking next year, but down the road, this area will be going through a renaissance as the rest of downtown is too. Okay. As you see more and more, the development downtown is— the, the skylight downtown is changing, and, and, uh, and this is part of that change. All for the question? All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Okay, we have, uh, 6C. This is variance 2025. This is referring to 430 Rockford Street. At this time, I will close the council meeting, open the public hearing. Mr. Warkentin, could you please introduce this file?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. File— variance file V-2025-03 for 430 Rockford Street. The applicant for the variance is [name withheld] of Smith Neufeld Jodoin LLP. The owners of the property are [names withheld]. Purpose of the variance is threefold. Firstly, to permit a detached accessory building to have a rear yard setback of 4.1 feet, whereas the RR rural residential zone requires a minimum setback of 5 feet. Secondly, to permit a detached accessory building to have a side yard setback of 3.7 feet, whereas the RR rural residential zone requires a minimum setback of 5 feet. Thirdly, to permit a minimum lot width of 70 feet, whereas the minimum lot width of the RR, rural residential zone, is 100 feet. The purpose of this application is to bring this property into compliance in order to facilitate a pending sale. Notices as are required under the Planning Act have been issued. There is no written correspondence on file. Recommendation from The recommendation from administration is for council to approve this variance application.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warkentin. Is the applicant present today? Okay. Seeing no one, is there anyone here with comments, questions, or objections to this file? I see nothing. I'll ask one more time. Is there anyone here with comments, questions, or objections to this file? Seeing none, I will close the public hearing, open the council meeting. Council, how would you like to proceed?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Seconded by Councillor Hiebert. Go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. As, uh, there are no objections here, administration has, uh, recommended that we approve the variance, and the fact that this building has been here for a substantial amount of time and has not negatively negatively affected anybody. I don't see any reason why we cannot approve this variance.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Anything further?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: I was at this location this morning and had a look, and it's not encroaching on anybody's property, and I understand, you know, in order for the pending sale that this variance goes through, so I don't have an issue with it.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Anything in closing? Nothing further. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Okay, council, we've got no delegations, reports, recommendations. We'll move to 9A, accounts payable, back of the book. All had a chance to review. Looking for a motion to approve. Councillor Hiebert, seconded by Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: No comments.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Call for the question. All those in favor? Where's Councillor Hiebert when you need him? We've got excavator licenses. Looking for a motion to approve. Second by Councillor Penner. Any comments?

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I can't express this as eloquently as Councillor Bill Hiebert, so I won't even try. I just hope we approve these excavator licenses.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Yeah, I hope so too. Anything No. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Is there any, any questions of council at this time? Okay, seeing none, we'll move to number 11. This is correspondence petitions. We've got the Steinbach Manitoba 55+ Games 2005 Committee request for sponsorship. Council, how would you like to proceed? Take his information? Okay, we've got the Southeast Event Centre Farmers Market. Council, how would you like to proceed?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: What do we need to— is this just a motion or resolution or—

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Administration would recommend if council has no concerns that the resolution be approved indicating exactly that to the the applicants or the requesters.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Yeah, make a motion to approve. Second by Councillor Penner. Go ahead, Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Um, I love this idea of having a farmers market downtown at, uh, on the event center parking lot. I'm sure it will be very well received. Uh, there's 2 sides to that. All for, you know, small businesses to be able to sell their products, I think is excellent. And also, I think it's a great service to have in our city for people to be able to go pick up fresh produce and whatever else is offered. So I think this is a great idea, and I think it's just one of the many benefits we'll see to having the event centre downtown.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. There's no better way to support local and support Canadian than at a farmers market, and it's a great incubator for local businesses as well. So I think it's appropriate on this dark Tariff Tuesday I hope that we bring some light of how there are local businesses that are wanting to thrive in Steinbach.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, great. Council, anything further? Anything closing?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Council, I agree. I think this is long overdue. I think we've needed a downtown farmers market for many, many years, and I'm excited to see this happen. So call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We've got, uh, 11C, the Seine River Watershed District minutes of January '21. Council, would you like to proceed, take his information at this time? And we've got the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee South Subcommittee minutes of February 10, 2025. Council, would you like to take his information at this time too? Mm-hmm. There's no other business. Looking for a motion to adjourn. Councillor Penner, seconded by Councillor Mr. Penner, call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Next regular council meeting is on Tuesday, March 18th, 2025 at 7:30. Thank you.
